sources.headline: Meta fined $25bn for 'lies' over user data privacy
sources.text: Meta, the company behind Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp has been hit with the largest ever fine against it for its business practices.A judge in New Mexico on Wednesday ordered the company to pay $25bn (£18.6bn) following a two-week trial earlier this year that found it had spent years lying to the public about how it handled Facebook user data."The lies extend beyond Facebook's data practices as well," the judge said, adding they went to "the heart of Facebook's core business practices".Meta's head lawyer CJ Mahoney said the ruling made it "all but impossible to do business in the state of New Mexico". The company intends to appeal, a move Mahoney said will be successful.The fine is the largest to date against Meta, which has either been fined or agreed to settle several other lawsuits this year, including an $18bn deal with California over child safety.New Mexico's lawsuit stemmed from the role of Meta, then still doing business as Facebook, in what became known as the Cambridge Analytica scandal.That firm utilised data and information from millions of Facebook users as part of its work in political consulting, including on work related to the 2016 US Presidential election, which saw Donald Trump elected for the first time.New Mexico had also accused Meta of intentionally misleading the public on how it benefitted from content that included hate speech, and how such rules against it were enforced. The jury found the company had intentionally misled the public on those claims, too. Meta disputed those accusations. "At its core, this lawsuit seeks to impose a tax on speech to enforce new rules for what people can say online," Mahoney added.Lawyers for New Mexico sued the company over many statements Meta executives had made over the years that user data was never shared with or accessed by third parties without a user's permission, when in reality it had been.They claimed that the entire population of the state, roughly two million people, was impacted by Meta's dishonesty regarding the way it controlled user data. A jury found that Meta had violated state laws more than 40 million times."For too long, powerful technology companies have operated as though their size and influence put them beyond the reach of the law," New Mexico Attorney General Raúl Torrez said on Wednesday. "Today's result makes clear that no corporation is too powerful to be held accountable."The state lawyers sought up to $40bn in fines against Meta. Meta had argued anything beyond $3.4bn would be unconstitutional. Judge Francis Mathew on Wednesday was direct in his decision to fine Meta an amount roughly equal to its profits each quarter.He said Meta's violations of law and misrepresentations to the public about how their Facebook data was used and shared were "willful" and spanned "more than 11 years", stretching from 2010 to 2021. Communications between senior executives, including Mark Zuckerberg, were "designed to mislead the public", Judge Mathew wrote in his order.While the full amount of the penalty against Meta, based on thousands of violations of state law, was calculated as $219bn, Judge Mathew reduced the penalty to the $25bn fine.It follows a $5bn fine levied by the US Federal Trade Commission in 2019 against the company over its data privacy practices.New Mexico has been one of Meta's most notable adversaries in court. The state this year also fined Meta almost $1bn for misleading the public about the safety of its social media platforms for children.The judge overseeing that lawsuit ultimately compared Meta to an industrial polluter of the air, with its form of pollution being "the psychological harm and sexual exploitation of children".As large as the fines against Meta are, the company is spending much more on infrastructure as it works to catch up with other tech companies in the artificial intelligence (AI) race.Zuckerberg said during a call with financial analysts that Meta's consumer-focused AI tool Muse was already being used by 10 million people. "Growing Muse to serve billions of people is both our mission and our strategy," Zuckerberg said. To that end, Meta expects to spend at least $135bn this year on mostly AI projects, but could spend up to $145bn.The company is spending so much on AI that it reported negative cash flow of more than $2bn - an apparent first for Meta since it listed on the public stock market 14 years ago, according to a BBC review of its past financial documents.Cash flow represents the money a company retains after paying for operations and investments. So, Meta is now spending more than it brings in, even as it brings in more money than ever.Meta's revenue increased 26% for July to September compared to a year ago, hitting $64.5bn. Its profits also tripled to $9.8bn.Still, the company intends to spend more on AI investments. Meta's chief financial officer Susan Li announced a new stock split on the call, in which existing Meta shareholders will receive one new share on non-voting stock. Li said the new class of stock was not yet intended for one specific investment, but she alluded to ongoing costs related to AI and said the company could use "more funding flexibility" next year.

sources.headline: Judge orders Meta to pay $25bn in fines for Facebook privacy violations
sources.text: A jury found Meta guilty of lying to Facebook users in ⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠New Mexico about access to their data.A United States judge has ordered Meta to pay $25bn after a jury found the company misled Facebook users about privacy violations, marking the biggest fine ever against the tech giant.New Mexico state District Judge Francis Mathew issued the ruling on Wednesday.Recommended Stories list of 3 itemslist 1 of 3Mexico to force Meta, TikTok, and X to better protect minors on platformlist 2 of 3Meta employees say Lula’s accounts restricted in Brazil election: Reportlist 3 of 3Why social media has become an election issue in Brazil’s presidential raceend of list“Facebook promised users that they (the users) controlled their data. This was false,” he said.Last month, a jury found Meta responsible for more than 43 million violations of New Mexico’s consumer protection laws. New Mexico Attorney General Raul Torrez highlighted that the decision was one of the largest state verdicts against a company in US history.“This judgement should be a signal, an unambiguous message, to Silicon Valley,” Torrez said at a news conference.New Mexico Attorney General Raul Torrez discusses a judgement in the state’s Facebook case during a news conference in Albuquerque, New Mexico, on Wednesday [Susan Montoya Bryan/AP]Meta lawyer Matt Nicholson argued in court that a sum as high as $40bn would be “shocking to the conscience”, while a lawyer for New Mexico, Randi McGinn, urged standing up to “tech titans who think they are bulletproof and can do whatever they want”.“The jury didn’t make findings that any New Mexican heard or saw these statements, or was harmed by them,” Nicholson argued during a hearing held early this month.Torrez told reporters following the verdict that all the money awarded would go into a fund for the state’s education system.The amount awarded in the case far exceeds the $5bn fine that the Federal Trade Commission levied against Facebook in 2019.New Mexico accused Meta of misleading users about who could access their personal information and how harmful content was handled on its platforms. Jurors found that 26 of 29 statements made by Meta and its leadership on privacy and content moderation were misleading.Meta plans to appeal the verdict, potentially reducing the final payment amount.In a statement, CJ Mahoney, Meta’s chief legal officer, said the company is confident it will win on appeal.“This ruling, and the Attorney General’s approach to this enforcement, makes it all but impossible to do business in the state of New Mexico,” Mahoney said. “At its core, this lawsuit seeks to impose a tax on speech to enforce new rules for what people can say online.”The lawsuit, filed in 2021, stemmed partly from revelations that Cambridge Analytica, a British political consulting firm that is now defunct, had obtained personal data from as many as 87 million Facebook users without their consent and used it to develop targeted political advertisements. Its clients included President Donald Trump’s 2016 presidential campaign.The case, a major setback for the tech giant, marks the second legal defeat for Meta in New Mexico in six months. In March, a jury found the company misled users about the safety of young people on Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp, ordering it to pay $375m in civil penalties. Meta was later ordered to make an additional $567m payment into a state fund for teen mental health and was required to implement measures to protect young users.

Meta fined $25 billion in New Mexico over Cambridge Analytica scandal 
 
  Technology   
 A New Mexico judge ordered Meta to pay $25 billion after a jury found the company deceived users in a case linked to the Cambridge Analytica scandal, media reported Wednesday. The ruling follows an $18 billion settlement with 48 other states over similar claims. Meta called the penalty “a tax on speech.”   
 
 
 
 
Issued on: 21/10/2026 - 23:21
    3 min Reading time   
  Share     
 
  By:  
 
  FRANCE 24       
 
     
 The penalty comes a couple of months after Meta agreed to pay $18 billion to settle claims brought by 48 other states, including allegations tied to Cambridge Analytica © Paul Faith, AFP    
 
A New Mexico judge ruled Wednesday that Meta must pay $25 billion to the state after a jury found last month that the social media giant had deceived users in a case related to the Cambridge Analytica scandal, according to media reports. 
The penalty comes a couple of months after Meta agreed to pay $18 billion to settle claims brought by 48 other states, including allegations tied to Cambridge Analytica. 
Meta slammed the case as "a tax on speech." 
"This ruling... makes it all but impossible to do business in the state of New Mexico," Meta said in a statement. "We are confident we will prevail on appeal." 
Cambridge Analytica was a political consulting firm found to have improperly harvested personal data from millions of Facebook users for targeted political advertising, notably during the 2016 US presidential election. 
Read moreFake AI images of protester go viral after woman punched at Trump's Ohio rally 
Revelations at the time showed that the firm had obtained data gathered through a personality quiz app called "thisisyourdigitallife," which was installed by about 270,000 users but also collected information on their friends. 
In total, the app reached roughly 87 million Facebook users worldwide. 
Facebook learned in December 2015 that Cambridge Analytica had acquired the data but did not disclose it publicly until 2018, after a whistleblower came forward, sparking a major political scandal. 
Jurors in the New Mexico trial found that the misconduct affected all of the state's more than 2.1 million residents. 
"We disagree with the verdict and will continue to defend ourselves against efforts to distort our record," a Meta spokesperson said in a statement in September. 
New Mexico Attorney General Raul Torrez hailed the ruling as a "historic" win. 
This case was "about whether corporations can mislead consumers about what happens to their personal information without facing meaningful consequences. New Mexicostood its ground," Torrez said in a statement. 
Read more'The harms have come to outweigh the benefits' of social media, researcher says 
Penalties pile up  
Meta has faced a slew of lawsuits in recent months.  
Earlier this year, New Mexico won nearly $1 billion in combined penalties against Metain a separate case over harms to children. 
In March, a jury in that case ordered Meta to pay $375 million after finding the company liable for endangering children by making them vulnerable to predators on its platforms, among other harms. 
In August, a judge ordered Meta to implement product changes and pay an additional $567 million to the state to fund the treatment and prevention of harms caused by Facebook and Instagram. 
That same month, Meta agreed to pay up to $17.7 billion to 52 US states, plus Washington, DC, to settle claims that it deliberately engineered its platforms to hook young users, misled the public about the risks and unlawfully collected data from children under 13. 
As part of that settlement, Meta agreed to make significant changes to Facebook and Instagram accounts used by teenagers, and portions of the settlement hinge on other major social media companies agreeing to similar changes. 
In September, TikTok agreed to pay Alabama at least $100 million and enact limits for teen users, avoiding a trial over claims related to child safety on the platform. 
TikTok previously settled other cases that were headed for trial, including a Los Angeles lawsuit brought by a young woman and a suit from a Kentucky school district. 
In a landmark trial that concluded in March, Meta and YouTube were convicted by a Los Angeles jury, which found both companies were responsible for a teenager's social media addiction. 
That jury awarded the teenager $6 million.  
(FRANCE 24 with AFP)

Meta to pay New Mexico a historic US$25 billion in Cambridge Analytica Facebook case

The company was accused of lying to Facebook users about its privacy policies and how it handled their data in the wake of the scandal

Bloomberg
Published: 3:08am, 22 Oct 2026Updated: 4:25am, 22 Oct 2026

Meta Platforms was ordered to pay a groundbreaking US$25 billion civil penalty to the state of New Mexico in a consumer deception case spurred by the Cambridge Analytica scandal.

The fine issued by state court Judge Francis Mathew is among the largest verdicts issued in US legal history.

The award comes after a jury in Santa Fe determined that Meta had violated the state’s consumer protection over 43 million times based on widely viewed deceptive statements made by the company and its top executives about how it handled hate speech and user data.

Under New Mexico’s Unfair Practices Act, Mathew could issue penalties of up to US$5,000 per violation.

The two-week trial in the First Judicial District Court of New Mexico centred on claims by Attorney General Raul Torrez that Meta had lied to Facebook users about its privacy policies and how it handled their data in the wake of the Cambridge Analytica leak almost a decade ago.

Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg stands outside the West Wing of the White House in September. Photo: EPA

The attorney general also advanced claims that the company deceived the public about content moderation decisions and its hate speech policies, pointing to evidence that certain high-profile accounts were not subject to the same scrutiny as ordinary users.

Jurors saw video deposition testimony from Chief Executive Officer Mark Zuckerberg and former chief operating officer Sheryl Sandberg.

Meta has been willing to pay large sums to settle cases involving the Cambridge Analytica leak, which involved a political consulting firm using ill-gotten data on millions of Facebook users to target voters for Donald Trump before the 2016 election.

The Menlo Park, California, company paid out US$5 billion to settle with the Federal Trade Commission in 2019, and signed a US$725 million settlement in 2022 to resolve a consumer class action.

Meta paid US$459 million in an agreement this summer to resolve cases from 46 states and two territories.

But New Mexico has been an especially costly thorn in the side of Meta, opting out of state AG coalitions prosecuting the company and instead going it alone.

The penalty award for New Mexico comes months after the state became the first in the nation to win a jury verdict against Meta over claims that Facebook and Instagram harm teen mental health and foster child sexual exploitation.

That trial from earlier this year saw a US$375 million civil penalty followed by an additional US$567 million payment Meta must make to the state to set up programmes to combat the youth mental health crisis.

sources.headline: Meta fined $25b in US for deceiving users about Facebook privacy
sources.text: A judge has ordered Meta to pay New Mexico $US25 billion ($35.6 billion) after a jury found the company liable for deceiving users about privacy on Facebook, marking the biggest fine ever against the tech giant.Facebook's deception was intentional and executives consistently misled users about how the platform worked, state District Court Judge Francis J Mathew wrote in his ruling on Wednesday local time."Facebook promised users that they [the users] controlled their data. This was false," he said.Raúl Torrez discusses the judgment during a news conference in Albuquerque. (AP: Susan Montoya Bryan)Jurors in September found Meta liable for more than 43 million violations of New Mexico consumer protection laws for making misleading public statements about how it handled users' personal data. The case was brought after political consulting firm Cambridge Analytica harvested Facebook data to generate targeted political ads during the 2016 election season.The award will serve as a warning to tech companies that New Mexico will hold them accountable, state Attorney-General Raúl Torrez said at a news conference."This judgment should be a signal, an unambiguous message, to Silicon Valley," he said.Meta said the ruling and Mr Torrez's office's approach to enforcement "makes it all but impossible to do business in the state of New Mexico"."At its core, this lawsuit seeks to impose a tax on speech to enforce new rules for what people can say online. We are confident we will prevail on appeal," CJ Mahoney, the company's chief legal officer, said in a statement.Meta also reported on Wednesday better-than-expected quarterly revenue of $US64.6 billion ($92 billion), ahead of Wall Street estimates of $US63.37 billion ($90.32 billion). New Mexico goes it aloneIn August, Meta reached a settlement with nearly all states and territories — except New Mexico and Florida — to pay $US18 billion ($25.6 billion) and add stronger child-safety measures to its Facebook and Instagram platforms.The settlement ended a trial over teenage social media addiction and resolved a pivotal case years in the making that sought to hold the tech giant accountable for the role its platforms played in undermining children's mental health.The effort targeted features designed to grab young people's attention.New Mexico did not join the multistate settlement, choosing to go after the company on its own.During the trial, prosecutors cited a 2010 Washington Post op-ed from Facebook CEO Mark Zuckerberg, in which he wrote that the company did not sell user data."You have control over how your information is shared," Mr Zuckerberg said."We do not and never will sell any of your information to anyone."Attorneys for New Mexico had sought $US35 billion ($49.8 billlion) to $US40 billion ($57 billion), arguing that the company would only change its ways with a sum that affected its stock price.Meta's lawyers, meanwhile, argued that the state failed to prove the company made misleading statements about privacy and that content moderation harmed New Mexicans.They contended that the company should pay no more than $US3.4 billion ($4.8 billion), saying an award 10 times that or even more would violate due process, was unconstitutional and would not hold up on appeal.Although interest would accrue on the penalty during the appeal process, Meta could succeed in reducing the number of violations for which it is found liable.The $US25 billion ($35.6 billion) award far exceeds the $US5 billion ($7.1 billion) fine that the Federal Trade Commission levied against Facebook in 2019.Villanova University associate law professor Peter Ormerod said he was surprised by the size of the New Mexico judgment because previous legal settlements over Cambridge Analytica were much lower."It comes out to about $US12,000 [$17,000] per person in New Mexico, and that's just a very large number. It's quite unlike anything else we've seen," Mr Ormerod said.Under the New Mexico Constitution, fines for violations of consumer protection laws go toward state education spending.But it could take years before the state sees any of the money while the company appeals.Company argues that the state failed to prove harmThe state's case focused on accusations that Facebook deceived users about a breach stemming from a third-party personality quiz that harvested data from about 87 million profiles and sold it to Cambridge Analytica.The now-defunct firm's clients included Donald Trump's 2016 presidential campaign.Attorneys for New Mexico argued that the state's entire population, not just Facebook users, was deceived by the company.They also said Facebook allowed misinformation or violent content to proliferate.Meta, led by Mark Zuckerberg, says it plans to appeal. (Reuters: Carlos Barria)Meta attorneys vehemently denied the allegations, saying the company's content moderation policies were robust and that freedom of speech must be considered.They argued that the state failed to prove people were harmed by deceptive statements.In one of the tech giant's few wins, jurors found that the state did not prove Facebook made false claims about removing harmful content, including misinformation about the COVID-19 pandemic.During a video deposition, Mr Zuckerberg denied the state's claims that Facebook profited off harmful content.He said the company had to balance freedom of speech with content moderation.Attorneys for the company said it had changed its policies since the lawsuit was filed in 2021 and that it caught and removed an estimated 99 per cent of the content that violates its standards.AP

sources.headline: Meta ordered to pay US$25b to New Mexico after jury finds company misled consumers about data privacy
sources.text: NEW MEXICO - A judge in New Mexico ordered Meta Platforms on Oct 21 to pay the state US$25 billion (S$32 billion) after a jury found the company had misled consumers about the privacy of their data, hitting the company with one of the largest financial penalties in US history.The ruling came in a case stemming from allegations that Cambridge Analytica, a British political consulting firm involved in Donald Trump’s 2016 presidential campaign, obtained data from millions of Facebook users without their consent. New Mexico had sued Meta, accusing it of lying to Facebook users in New Mexico about who had access to their data.“Facebook’s wrongdoing – over the course of years and systematically broadcast to the public – goes to the heart of Facebook’s core business practices,” Judge Francis Mathew wrote in his order, which came more than three weeks after the verdict.Mathew found that a penalty of more than US$219 billion was warranted based on state law, but he reduced the figure to US$25 billion.In a statement, C.J. Mahoney, Meta’s chief legal officer, said the company is confident it will win on appeal.“This ruling, and the Attorney General’s approach to this enforcement, makes it all but impossible to do business in the state of New Mexico,” Mahoney said. “At its core, this lawsuit seeks to impose a tax on speech to enforce new rules for what people can say online.”New Mexico Attorney General Raúl Torrez said in a statement after the ruling the penalty was one of the largest financial penalties against a corporation in US history.Meta previously faced a US$5 billion penalty from the US Federal Trade Commission in 2019 over the Cambridge Analytica scandal.Six other states settled their lawsuits against Meta related to Cambridge Analytica for US$459.2 million as part of a US$17.1 billion multistate settlement the company reached in August to resolve states’ claims that the company’s platforms had harmed teen mental health.Lawsuit filed five years agoNew Mexico’s attorney general had sued Meta in 2021 following revelations that Cambridge Analytica had harvested personal data from as many as 87 million Facebook users through a third-party app.The state accused Meta of lying to Facebook users in New Mexico about who had access to their data, how the company handles hate speech and misinformation posted on the platform and other internal policies. The company knew that third parties had broad access to users’ personal data, and it tolerated hate speech or other harmful content when it benefited the company’s bottom line, the state said.Cambridge Analytica, now defunct, worked for Trump’s successful presidential campaign in 2016, and gained access to the personal information from millions of Facebook accounts for the purposes of voter profiling and targeting. It obtained that information without users’ consent from a researcher who had been allowed by Facebook to deploy an app on its social media network.“It has been a long time coming holding Big Tech accountable,” Torrez told a press conference in Albuquerque after Wednesday’s ruling. “I think today’s judgment is a clear break with that past and a very clear warning to those in this space and beyond that we intend to protect our people and protect our consumers.”Analyst Gil Luria, head of technology research at D.A. Davidson & Co, called the ruling costly but unlikely to impact the company’s value.“Meta is worth nearly two trillion dollars, and will likely continue to appeal these cases and drag them out,” Luria said.Experts expect long appeal fightLegal experts and financial analysts said the penalty was likely to face a lengthy battle on appeal.Jurors on September 25 found that 26 of 29 statements made by the company and its leadership on those issues were misleading. They said the company had committed more than 43 million violations of New Mexico’s consumer protection laws, based on the number of Facebook users or New Mexico residents who were the audience for each misleading statement.State law allows a penalty of up to US$5,000 per violation, and directs that all of the money go to New Mexico’s school system, Torrez told reporters after the verdict. At a hearing on Oct 1, Randi McGinn, a lawyer for New Mexico, had asked Mathew to award the state between US$35 billion and US$40 billion, saying that would be supported by the US Constitution’s protections on due process and the jury’s verdict.“This court should speak to Meta in the only language it understands, which is money, and the value of its stock price,” McGinn said.In court filings, Meta urged Mathew to cap the penalties at US$3.45 billion, saying a higher penalty ran the risk of scaring businesses out of the state. The evidence showed that Meta does not sell user data and New Mexico did not prove that any consumer had actually been misled, the company said in court filings.Daryl Lim, an associate dean at Penn State Dickinson Law, said that while the US Constitution generally protects against excessive fines, because of the way New Mexico law is written, the large size of the penalty does not automatically mean it could be overturned.Two juries sided with stateThe verdict was the second in six months by a Santa Fe jury in a lawsuit brought by the state of New Mexico against Meta Platforms.In the first trial, which ended in March, a Santa Fe jury ​found Meta misled users ⁠about young users’ safety on its Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp platforms and ordered the company to pay US$375 million in civil penalties. After a second phase of that trial, a judge directed the company to pay US$567 million into a New Mexico fund for teen mental health and ordered Meta to implement measures to protect teen Facebook and Instagram users in New Mexico.
